summary: Adds several control operators to the Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), which RFC 8610 standardized. They include .plus, .cat, and .det for building constants, .abnf and .abnfb for embedding ABNF grammars, and .feature for flagging use of a non-basic feature. These were not ready when RFC 8610 was finished.

eli5.summary: A language for describing data gets a few new tools in its toolbox, so you can describe more kinds of things.

questions: how to concatenate strings in cddl
how to use abnf in cddl
subtitle: Six new CDDL operators for computing constants, embedding ABNF grammars and flagging extensions.

tldr.problem: CDDL, the language for describing CBOR and JSON data, had no way to compute literals, no way to reuse existing ABNF grammars, and no way to mark use of an extension. These operators were not ready when RFC 8610 was finished.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC adds six control operators: .plus, .cat and .det build constants; .abnf and .abnfb embed ABNF for text and byte strings; .feature marks a use of a non-basic feature.
tldr.outcome: CDDL specifications can now compute numbers and strings, reuse ABNF written for other IETF protocols, and let validators report extensions instead of failing them outright. The operators are registered with IANA.

today: RFC 9165 is a Proposed Standard and has not been obsoleted or updated, so it remains the definition of these six operators on top of RFC 8610.

sections.title: Control Operators Beyond RFC 8610
sections.content:
The Concise Data Definition Language (CDDL), standardized in RFC 8610, uses control operators as its main extension point. This RFC defines six operators that were not yet ready when RFC 8610 was completed.

The RFC borrows two terms from RFC 8610: the target is the left-hand operand of an operator and the controller is the right-hand operand. It also treats text strings and byte strings as two separate types that are together called strings.

  • .plus: numeric addition
  • .cat: string concatenation
  • .det: string concatenation with dedenting first
  • .abnf and .abnfb: ABNF for text strings and byte strings
  • .feature: names a feature that is being used
sections.eli5: CDDL is a way to write down what a piece of data should look like. This document adds six extra tools to that writing kit.

sections.title: Computed Literals: .plus, .cat and .det
sections.content:
CDDL had no way to compute a literal. These three operators cover the common cases. As with every control operator, targets and controllers are types, so the result is formally a function of the cross-product of the two types. Not all tools may be able to work with non-unique targets or controllers.

.plus adds the numeric values of target and controller. Both MUST be numeric. If one is a floating point number and the other an integer, the sum is converted to the type of the target, and converting a float to an integer takes the floor (rounding towards negative infinity). The RFC's example defines a generic group interval<BASE> with labels BASE, BASE .plus 1 and BASE .plus 2, so two intervals can sit in one map without label clashes.

.cat concatenates two strings. Both MUST be strings, the result has the type of the target, and the concatenation works on the bytes. If the target is a text string, the result MUST be valid UTF-8. A handy idiom is a text target with a byte-string controller written in text form, which makes embedded newlines easy to read.

.det works like .cat, except that both operands are first independently dedented. It is short for "dedenting cat".
sections.eli5: One tool adds numbers, one glues two pieces of text together, and one first tidies the left margin of both pieces and then glues them. It saves you from writing the same thing out by hand.

sections.title: How Dedenting Works
sections.content:
Multi-line string literals, such as embedded ABNF, need to be flush left, yet indented source is easier to read. The RFC defines dedenting in two steps.

  1. Find the smallest number of leading space characters present in all the non-blank lines.
  2. Remove exactly that many leading spaces from each line. Blank lines may have fewer (or no) leading spaces, in which case all their leading space is removed.

To dedent only one operand, use .det with an empty string, for example "" .det rhs. In the construct lhs .cat ("" .det rhs), only rhs is dedented.
sections.eli5: Imagine a paragraph that is pushed in from the edge of the page. Dedenting slides the whole paragraph left until the line sticking out least touches the edge.

sections.title: Embedded ABNF
sections.content:
Many IETF protocols define the allowed values of their text strings in ABNF (RFC 5234 and RFC 7405, together simply called "ABNF" here). Without CDDL support, that ABNF would usually have to be translated into a regular expression, if that is possible at all. Like regular expressions before them, ABNF grammars are added with control operators.

Two operators exist because ABNF can describe bytes or Unicode text. .abnfb treats the string as a sequence of bytes. .abnf treats it as a sequence of Unicode code points represented as UTF-8 text. Both can be applied to targets of either string type. The controller MUST be a string, and if it is a byte string it MUST be valid UTF-8.

Several small issues have fixed answers:

  • ABNF defines a list of rules, not a single expression. The controller must be one valid ABNF element, followed by zero or more valid rules separated from it by a newline.
  • ABNF needs newlines, which are tedious in CDDL text strings. The workaround is .cat with a byte string in text form, and a single line feed is accepted as a newline: CRLF = %x0A / %x0D.0A.
  • Every rule referenced must be defined in each controller string. There is no implicit import of core rules from RFC 5234, so shared rules such as DIGIT are composed with .cat or .det.

The RFC's worked example uses ABNF from RFC 3339 to define the CBOR date tags 1004 (full-date) and 0 (date-time).
sections.eli5: Many grammar rules were already written in another notation. Instead of rewriting them, you can paste them in and tell CDDL to read them, as long as you include every rule they need.

sections.title: Marking Extensions with .feature
sections.content:
Validation usually gives a yes or no answer. In fast-changing environments that is too simple. A specification can leave an extension point and still accept extensions, while marking them as extensions.

The .feature control annotates the target as using the feature named by the controller, usually a string. A validating tool may mark the instance as using that feature. A tool's diagnostics might show the controller as the feature name and the target as the feature detail. If the target has too much detail, the controller can be an array: the first element is the feature name and the second is the detail.

The RFC argues that leaving out the extension point makes any use of an extension wholesale invalid, while leaving it in unmarked hides mistakes, such as writing the label "organisation" instead of "organization". Its examples cover map extensibility, type extensibility and a JSON/CBOR switch using JC<J,C> = J .feature "json" / C .feature "cbor" for SenML.

A tool may simply report the features used, or may take arguments to accept some features and reject others. The language currently has no way to enforce mutually exclusive use of features, and the RFC says it remains to be seen whether the enable/disable approach leads to new idioms.
sections.eli5: It is like a sticky note saying "this part uses something extra". Checkers can still accept the data, but they can point at the part that is not standard.

sections.title: IANA and Security Considerations
sections.content:
IANA has registered all six names (.plus, .cat, .det, .abnf, .abnfb, .feature) in the "CDDL Control Operators" registry, with this RFC as the reference.

The security considerations of RFC 8610 apply. The RFC notes that formal description techniques can simplify a specification but sometimes also complicate it, which can lead to security problems in implementations and in the specification itself. ABNF should be used judiciously, and overly complex ("cute") constructions should be avoided.
sections.eli5: Fancy rule-writing can make mistakes easier to hide, so keep your rules simple.

viz.caption: ADDITION TO A BASE VALUE (RFC 9165, FIGURE 1)

data.title: interval group with .plus
data.code:
interval<BASE> = (
  BASE => int             ; lower bound
  (BASE .plus 1) => int   ; upper bound
  ? (BASE .plus 2) => int ; tolerance
)

X = 0
Y = 3
rect = {
  interval<X>
  interval<Y>
}
